name: Pashalik of Timbuktu (Arma)
summary: A West African state founded after Morocco's 1591 conquest of Songhai, ruled by the Arma, descendants of the Moroccan soldiers, until it became a Tuareg tributary and was replaced in 1833.

knownFor.label: Arma casbahs
knownFor.note: Garrisons of Moroccan-descended soldiers across the Middle Niger.

knownFor.label: Judar Pasha
knownFor.note: Led the Moroccan expedition that destroyed Songhai.

location.value: The middle Niger valley, roughly from Gao to Djenné, centred on Timbuktu in today's Mali.

governmentType.value: A Moroccan-founded pashalik: a pasha, chosen by the army soldiers, ruled as military governor; the Arma (descendants of the Moroccan soldiers) held power.
governmentType.source: EBSCO Research Starters: Songhai Empire Dissolves

keyRulers.value: Judar Pasha led the 1591 expedition; later pashas include Mahmud ibn Zarqun (1591-95), Mahmud Longo (1604-12) and Ali ben Abdallah al-Tilimsani (1612-17).

succession.value: From 1591 to 1833 Timbuktu had 167 pashas, and only a few lasted more than a year.

stability.value: Constant feuds and internal strife; the position rotated among three main Arma factions.

armyAndTech.value: A Moroccan army with firearms defeated the Songhai at Tondibi in 1591; the Arma lived in garrisons (casbahs) scattered across the Middle Niger.
armyAndTech.source: EBSCO Research Starters: Songhai Empire Dissolves

majorWars.value: War against the Songhai remnant in Dendi; a treaty in 1630 ended the aim of conquering all Songhai, and in 1639 an Arma army sacked the Dendi capital Loulami.
majorWars.source: EBSCO Research Starters: Songhai Empire Dissolves

territoryChange.value: Founded 1591 after the Moroccan conquest of Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné; from about 1770 the Tuareg took Gao and in 1787 entered Timbuktu and made the pashalik their tributary.

alliancesRivals.value: Nominally tied to Morocco (Sultan Moulay al-Rashid sent a force in 1671; Moulay Ismail in 1689); rivals were the Songhai of Dendi and the Tuareg.

sharedIdentity.value: The Moroccan soldiers intermarried with Songhai women, creating the Arma, a distinct soldier-ruler group.
sharedIdentity.source: EBSCO Research Starters: Songhai Empire Dissolves

neighbours.value: The Songhai of Dendi, the Tuareg, Bambara states and Morocco across the Sahara.

riseSignals.value: The Moroccan invasion of the Songhai Empire in 1590-91 and the capture of Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné.

declineSignals.value: By the mid-18th century the pashalik was in total eclipse; the Tuareg made it a tributary in 1787.

outcome.value: Disestablished in 1833 and succeeded by the Caliphate of Hamdullahi.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Pashalik of Timbuktu and Arma people; EBSCO Research Starters: Songhai Empire Dissolves. Read as search excerpts only, 16 Nov 2026.

overallCertainty.value: The status of Morocco's control is given differently by sources (governorate until 1612, 1621 or 1603), so the political status dates are disputed; the end of Arma rule is given as 1737 in one source.
